The Temperley-Lieb tower and the Weyl algebra
Matthew Harper, Peter Samuelson

Abstract
. We define a monoidal category 𝐖 \operatorname{\mathbf{W}} and a closely related 2-category 𝟐 ​ 𝐖 ​ 𝐞 ​ 𝐲 ​ 𝐥 \operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}} using diagrammatic methods. We show that 𝟐 ​ 𝐖 ​ 𝐞 ​ 𝐲 ​ 𝐥 \operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}} acts on the category 𝐓𝐋 := ⨁ n TL n − mod \mathbf{TL}:=\bigoplus_{n}\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod} of modules over Temperley-Lieb algebras, with its generating 1-morphisms acting by induction and restriction. The Grothendieck groups of 𝐖 \operatorname{\mathbf{W}} and a third category we define 𝐖 ∞ \operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty} are closely related to the Weyl algebra. We formulate a sense in which K 0 ​ ( 𝐖 ∞ ) K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}) acts asymptotically on K 0 ​ ( 𝐓𝐋 ) K_{0}(\mathbf{TL}) .

†
†

2020
Mathematics Subject Classification:
16D90

1.
Introduction

A sequence
\{A_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}\}
of algebras is called a
tower of algebras
if it is equipped with algebra homomorphisms
\iota_{m,n}:A_{m}\otimes A_{n}\to A_{m+n}
satisfying an obvious associativity condition. Towers of algebras arise quite naturally in representation theory – the prototypical example is the sequence
\Bbbk S_{n}
of group algebras of the symmetric groups. The representation theory of algebras in a tower is most naturally studied simultaneously; more precisely, the category
\mathcal{A}:=\bigoplus_{n}A_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
has natural endofunctors induction (
\operatorname{Ind}
) and restriction (
\operatorname{Res}
), both along the maps
\iota:A_{n}\to A_{n+1}
. The monoidal subcategory of
\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf{Cat}}(\mathcal{A})
generated by induction and restriction tends to be interesting and deserves careful study.

In the example of the tower of symmetric groups, Khovanov
[
Kho14
]
used a diagrammatic construction to define the
Heisenberg category

\mathcal{H}^{K}
and proved that there is a monoidal functor
\mathcal{H}^{K}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf{Cat}}(\bigoplus_{n}S_{n}\mathrm{-mod})
. An action in this context maps an object
x\in\mathcal{H}^{K}
to a functor between categories of symmetric group representations. He proved that the Heisenberg algebra injects into the Grothendieck group of
\mathcal{H}^{K}
and conjectured they were isomorphic – this conjecture was proved recently in
[
BSW23
]
.

Other invariants of the Heisenberg category have also been attracting
recent attention. First, recall the
trace
of a category
\mathcal{C}
is defined as

\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{C}):=\frac{\mathbbm{k}\{\oplus_{X}\mathrm{End}(X)\mid X\in Ob(\mathcal{C})\}}{\{f\circ g-g\circ f\}}\,.

If
\mathcal{C}
is monoidal, then its trace is an algebra, and there is a
Chern character
(algebra) map
K_{0}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{C})
sending
[X]\mapsto\mathrm{Id}_{X}
. In
[
CLLS18
]
, Cautis, Lauda, Licata, and Sussan showed the trace of the Heisenberg category is the
\mathcal{W}_{1+\infty}
algebra. This provides an example of a category where the Chern character map is not an isomorphism; in this example, the trace is a much bigger, more interesting algebra.

Khovanov’s Heisenberg category was deformed to the quantum Heisenberg category
\mathcal{H}_{q}^{LS}
using Hecke algebras by Licata and Savage in
[
LS13
]
and this category was generalized further to
\mathcal{H}_{q,k}^{BSW}
by Brundan, Savage, and Webster in
[
BSW20b
]
. The traces of these categories were computed in
[
CLL+18
]
and
[
MS22
]
, and in both cases they are closely related to the
elliptic Hall algebra
of Burban and Schiffmann
[
BS12
]
.
Finally, in
[
BSW20a
]
Brundan, Savage, and Webster showed that the Heisenberg category
\mathcal{H}_{q}^{BSW}
can be used to construct 2-representations of Kac-Moody 2-categories, which was an a-priori more difficult problem.

This history of interesting results involving Heisenberg categories motivates the goal of the present paper: study symmetries of the representation category of the tower of Temperley-Lieb algebras
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
. Some progress towards this goal was made by Quinn in
[
Qui17
]
, who gave a partial diagrammatic description of a monoidal category which acts on

\mathbf{TL}:=\bigoplus_{n}\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
.

It turns out that the construction of a category acting on
\mathbf{TL}
is more subtle than one might expect from the Heisenberg category (for reasons we discuss later). Our construction actually involves three categories: a “universal” monoidal category
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
, a 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
, and an “asymptotic” monoidal category
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
. The universal category is used to construct the other two categories by imposing different sets of relations on endomorphisms of the tensor unit
\mathbbm{1}
. In other words, there are functors from
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,m)
and
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
which quotient out certain relations on morphisms. The resulting 2-category acts on
\mathbf{TL}
with its generating 1-morphisms acting by induction and restriction. We expect that
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
acts
“asymptotically” on
\mathbf{TL}
, but we leave the details of this to future work. In Section
8
, we discuss an asymptotic action of this category under the
K_{0}
functor.

Let
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
be the additive
\mathbb{C}(q)
-linear strict monoidal category generated by the objects
Q_{-}
and
Q_{+}
. Morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
are generated by oriented cups and caps, a disoriented cupcap, and endomorphisms of
\mathbbm{1}
given by integer-labeled boxes. Relations in this category are given in (
15
)-(
24
).

A key structural difference between the Heisenberg and Weyl categories is the existence of idempotent endomorphisms of the monoidal unit of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
called “idempotent bubbles”. The image of such an idempotent is a subobject of
\mathbbm{1}
in the Karoubi completion – the universal Weyl category – denoted
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. These bubbles are expressible in terms of the generating morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
, but there are no analogous morphisms in the present definition(s) of the Heisenberg category.

Theorem A

(Proposition
4.6
)
.

There is an isomorphism in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
:

\displaystyle Q_{-}\otimes Q_{+}\cong\left(Q_{+}\otimes Q_{-}\right)\oplus C_{0}\,.

This relation motivates the name for our category, since it is very closely related to the relation
xy=yx+1
in the Weyl algebra.

Remark 1.1
.

The class of the object
C_{0}
is an idempotent
[C_{0}]\neq[\mathbbm{1}]
in the Grothendieck group of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. However,
[C_{0}]
does
not
commute with
[Q_{+}]
or
[Q_{-}]
. For example, see equation (
60
).
∎

Remark 1.2
.

Based on the results of the present paper, we expect there exists an extension of the Heisenberg category (or, 2-category) that contains idempotent bubbles that act by projection onto isotypic components – finding the correct definition of this category seems to be an interesting but challenging question that we hope to return to in the future. If we identify
S_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
with
K^{{{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}}}(\mathrm{Hilb}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}^{2}))
, then we expect these idempotent bubbles should act geometrically as restriction of sheaves to fixed points. However, it is not clear whether there is a direct relation between the Heisenberg category and any of the Weyl categories introduced here – Remark
4.5
shows that the standard surjection from the Hecke algebra to the Temperley-Lieb algebra does not extend to a functor from the Heisenberg category to
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
.
∎

Another difference between the Heisenberg category and the category in our construction is the necessity to use a 2-categorical approach to define an action on a category of modules. In particular, the relations that naturally appear between morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
have constants that depend on
n
(i.e. they depend on which summand of
\mathbf{TL}=\bigoplus_{n}\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
the morphisms are acting on). These constants are encoded into the integer-labeled boxes and
act as rational functions whose denominators vanish for certain values of
n
, which means the action of an
m
-labeled box is only defined when
n
is large enough.
We therefore construct a 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
before considering an action on
\mathbf{TL}
. Each morphism category in
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
is defined as a quotient of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. Our first main result is the construction of this 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
which acts on
\mathbf{TL}
via induction and restriction.

Theorem B

(Theorem
6.2
)
.

There is a well-defined functor
\rho:\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
which maps
Q_{-}
to restriction,
Q_{+}
to induction, and
C_{k}
to the projection onto the isotypic simple component
W^{n}_{n-2k}
in
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
for each
n
.

Using this functor we describe spanning sets and bases of certain endomorphism spaces of 1-morphisms of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
.

We also define a quotient of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
called the
asymptotic Weyl category

\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
. We give a conjectural description of a subalgebra
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})^{\prime}\subset K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})
generated by the classes of
Q_{+},Q_{-}
, and the
C_{k}
by defining an algebra
\mathcal{K}
by generators and relations which surjects onto this subalgebra of
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})^{\prime}
(see Proposition
8.4
for a precise statement).

The monoidal category
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
is called “asymptotic” because we show
\mathcal{K}
“acts asymptotically” on
K_{0}(\mathbf{TL})
. Our notion of an
aysmptotic representation
is defined as an increasingly-filtered algebra acting on a decreasingly-filtered vector space, which defines an action of an algebra element on the
n
-th filtered component as
n\to\infty
, see Definition
8.8
. This action is defined such that it respects composition in the algebra (see Propostion
8.9
). It is in this way that
\mathcal{K}
“acts” on
K_{0}(\mathbf{TL})
despite
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
and
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
not admitting actions
on
\mathbf{TL}
in the usual sense. We expect that there is a categorification of this notion of asymptotic representation which lifts to
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
(or some subquotient category) acting asymptotically on
\mathbf{TL}
.

There are a number of avenues we intend to pursue in future work. In particular, we would like to describe the Grothendieck category of the 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
, which will require stronger basis theorems than we currently provide. We also plan to use skein-theoretic techniques and results to describe the trace of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
, which we expect to be closely related to Cherednik’s
double affine Hecke algebra
for
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
.

We hope to relate
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
,
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
, and
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
to other categories appearing in categorical representation theory. Since any object
V
in a monoidal category generates a tower of algebras as
\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes n})
, the asymptotic categorical representation theory of these may also be interesting.

An outline of the paper is as follows. We include a table of notation in Section
2
. In Section
3
, we provide background results about Temperley-Lieb algebras. We give a graphical description of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
in Section
4
, and prove some diagrammatic relations. In Section
5
we construct the 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
, and we prove it acts on
\mathbf{TL}
in Section
6
. In Section
7
we prove some basis theorems for morphisms spaces in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
and
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
. Finally, in Section
8
we give a conjectural description of the Grothendieck group of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
and show that it acts asymptotically on
K_{0}(\mathbf{TL})
. The appendix contains a summary of some of Quinn’s results from
[
Qui17
]
.

3.
The Temperley-Lieb Algebra

Fix a formal parameter
q
and ground field
{\mathbb{C}}(q)
. Let
V
be the 2-dimensional irreducible representation of
U=U_{q}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2})
and
W=V\wedge V
, which is a direct summand of
V^{\otimes 2}
. Let
\operatorname{TL}_{n}=\operatorname{End}_{U}(V^{\otimes n})
be the Temperley-Lieb algebra on
n\geq 0
strands. The algebra is generated by quasi-idempotents
e^{\prime}_{i}
for
i=1,\dots,n-1
, where

(1)

\displaystyle(e^{\prime}_{i})^{2}=(q+q^{-1})e^{\prime}_{i}=[2]e^{\prime}_{i}\,,

\displaystyle e^{\prime}_{i}e^{\prime}_{i\pm 1}e^{\prime}_{i}=e^{\prime}_{i}\,,

and
[2]=q+q^{-1}
. More generally, we write
[n]
for
\dfrac{q^{n}-q^{-n}}{q-q^{-1}}
. We denote the idempotent form of these generators by
e_{i}=e^{\prime}_{i}/[2]
, which satisfy
e_{i}^{2}=e_{i}
. The Temperley-Lieb diagram for the generator
e^{\prime}_{i}
is the cupcap over strands
i
and
i+1
. We use the convention that strand 1 is
on the right
and strand
n
is
on the left
. For example, the element
e_{1}\in\operatorname{TL}_{4}
is given in the diagram below.

\operatorname{TL}_{n}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}
is the
m=1

and for
x\in\operatorname{TL}_{n}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}
, we have
e_{n}^{\prime}xe_{n}^{\prime}=e_{n}^{\prime}\operatorname{ptr}_{n}(x)
.

We briefly recall the Jones-Wenzl idempotents. For each
n\geq 0
, there exists a unique
f^{(n)}\in\operatorname{TL}_{n}
which satisfies the following properties

•

f^{(n)}\neq 0
,

•

f^{(n)}f^{(n)}=f^{(n)}
,

•

e_{i}f^{(n)}=f^{(n)}e_{i}=0
for all
i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}
.

Let
f^{(0)}
denote the empty diagram and set
f^{(1)}
to be a single strand. For
n\geq 2
the Jones-Wenzl idempotents are defined by the recursive relation

(5)

\displaystyle f^{(n+1)}=f^{(n)}-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}f^{(n)}e_{n}f^{(n)}

where
f^{(n)}\in\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}
via the inclusion
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}
. These idempotents also satisfy the relation

(6)

\displaystyle\operatorname{ptr}_{n}(f^{(n)})=\frac{[n+1]}{[n]}f^{(n-1)}\,.

In some cases, it will be easier for us to use the notation
\cup_{i}
and
\cap_{i}
to describe Temperley-Lieb diagrams. For instance, we will consider the
\operatorname{TL}_{n+2}
-diagram
\cup_{n}f^{(n+1)}\cap_{n}
. Each of
\cup_{i}
and
\cap_{i}
indicates a cup or cap over strands
i
and
i+1
. In this way, the first
n-1
strands of
f^{(n+1)}
are to the right of
\cup_{n}
and the
n+1
-st strand of
f^{(n+1)}
is to the left of
\cup_{n}
(in the right to left labeling convention), and similarly for
\cap_{n}
. The expression
\cup_{n}f^{(n+1)}\cap_{n}
is equal to
e_{n+2}e_{n+1}f^{(n+1)}e_{n+1}
and may be drawn diagrammatically as

(7)

4.
The Universal Weyl Category

4.1.
Definition

We define an additive
\mathbb{C}(q)
-linear strict monoidal category
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
as follows. The set of objects is tensor generated by the objects
Q_{+}
and
Q_{-}
. An object in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
is a finite direct sum of
objects
Q_{\epsilon}=Q_{\epsilon_{\ell}}\otimes\dots\otimes Q_{\epsilon_{1}}
, where
\epsilon=\epsilon_{\ell}\cdots\epsilon_{1}\in\{+,-\}^{\ell}
. We denote the unit object by
\mathbbm{1}
, which corresponds to the empty sequence.

The space of morphisms
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}}(Q_{\epsilon},Q_{\epsilon^{\prime}})
is the
{\mathbb{C}}(q)
-module generated by diagrams

(8)

(9)

{k}

for
k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
modulo rel boundary isotopies. Notice that the last diagram
\boxed{k}
has no boundary components. We call such elementary diagrams boxes. The other diagram in (
9
) is called a (disoriented) cupcap. We refer to the non-solid components of cupcaps as doubled strands. The orientation at the endpoints of a diagram in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(Q_{\epsilon},Q_{\epsilon^{\prime}})
must agree with the signs in the sequences
\epsilon
and
\epsilon^{\prime}
, where
+
corresponds to
\uparrow
and
-
corresponds to
\downarrow
. Composition of morphisms is given by stacking diagrams. Diagrams without boundary components are endomorphisms of
\mathbbm{1}
.

Before stating the relations in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
, we make the following notational conveniences for
k\geq 0
.

(10)

Remark 4.1
.

The local relations we impose are significantly more complicated than in the Heisenberg category. We don’t have a satisfying explanation for this complexity, but our ansatz for imposing relations is “relations that hold in the action of the category should hold in the category itself.” The relations imposed will hold for both categories we construct from
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
in their actions on Temperley-Lieb modules.
∎

We impose the following local relations between morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
:

Remark 4.3
.

Relation (
24
) is somewhat complicated but we make use of it in the proof of Proposition
5.5
.
∎

Let
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
be the Karoubi envelope of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
. Thus, the objects of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
are pairs
(Q_{\epsilon},e)
, where
e:Q_{\epsilon}\to Q_{\epsilon}
is an idempotent. Morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
are triples
(f,e,e^{\prime})
where
f:Q_{\epsilon}\to Q_{\epsilon^{\prime}}
is a morphism in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
such that
f=e^{\prime}\circ f=f\circ e
. For each
k\geq 0
, let
C_{k}
be the image of the idempotent
{k}
in
\operatorname{End}(\mathbbm{1})
as an object in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
.

by taking the right trace of the former and resolving the counterclockwise circle. This shows that the cupcap is an idempotent in our category, and similarly for its dual. Let
Q_{\oplus}
denote the image of this projection on
Q_{+}^{\otimes 2}
as an object in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. The image of the dual cupcap is denoted
Q_{\ominus}
. Diagrammatically, we write
Q_{\oplus}
as the source and target of an isolated “doubled strand”. It is then natural write the projection and inclusion maps between
Q_{+}^{\otimes 2}
and
Q_{\oplus}
as factors of the cupcap:

4.2.
Basic Isomorphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}

There are several isomorphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
which follow from single relations together with idempotency of bubbles. We will suppress the tensor product from the notation to improve readability, i.e.
A\otimes B
is written as
AB
. For example,

(26)

\displaystyle C_{k}Q_{+}

\displaystyle\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\oplus C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k-1}

(27)

\displaystyle Q_{+}C_{k}

\displaystyle\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\oplus C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}

and similar identities involving
Q_{-}
follow from (
19
) and its rotation, and (
21
). In addition, invertiblity of
\boxed{0}
from (
22
), and (
18
) and (
23
) imply

(28)

\displaystyle C_{0}Q_{-}C_{0}Q_{+}C_{0}

\displaystyle\cong C_{0}\,.

The remaining isomorphism, which lends this category its name, is stated as a proposition.

Proposition 4.6
.

The following isomorphism holds in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
:

Q_{-+}\cong Q_{+-}\oplus C_{0}\,.

15
), adjoining (tracing) the left strands, and reflecting across a vertical axis, we observe that

Remark 4.7
.

In the Grothendieck group
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}})
the isomorphism in Proposition
4.6
becomes

(29)

[Q_{-}][Q_{+}]-[Q_{+}][Q_{-}]=[C_{0}]

a loosening of the defining relation of the Weyl algebra where
1
is replaced by a
noncentral
idempotent.

This isomorphism is analogous to one in the quantum Heisenberg categories
\mathcal{H}_{q,k}^{BSW}
with central charge
k
studied by
[
BSW20b
]
(which specialize to the quantum Heisenberg category of
[
LS13
]
by setting
k=-1
). In the Heisenberg categories with nonpositive central charge, there is an isomorphism

(30)

\displaystyle Q_{-+}^{H}\cong Q_{+-}^{H}\oplus\mathbbm{1}^{(-k)}

In the isomorphism of Proposition
4.6
, the object
C_{0}
on the right hand side is a subobject of
\mathbbm{1}
. In a rough sense, this behavior is “in between” the Heisenberg categories with central charges
k=0
and
k=-1
.
∎

Although the infinite sum identity is not a relation in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
, it appears naturally in the categorical representation of the Weyl category on the direct sum over
n
of
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-modules. On any module,
C_{k}
the image of
{k}
in
\mathbbm{1}
, acts as a projection onto certain isotypic simple module components and the sum over all such projections is the identity on any module. Since there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of simple modules for a given
n
, all but finitely many terms in this infinite sum vanish.
∎

5.
The Weyl 2-Category

As it is currently defined, the monoidal category
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
does not act on
\mathbf{TL}
, the sum over
n
of the categories of Temperley-Lieb modules. This is because the constants needed to define the action depend on
n
in an essential way. This means that to define the action we want, we need to use the 2-categorical point of view. In this section, we define the Weyl 2-category and compare isomorphisms which hold in the 2-category but not in the monoidal category. The action on
\bigoplus_{n}\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
is described precisely in the next section.

The Weyl 2-Category

The 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
is the Karoubi completion
1
1

1

By the Karoubi completion of a 2-category
\mathcal{C}
, we mean the 2-category with the same objects as
\mathcal{C}
, but whose morphism categories are the Karoubi completions of those of
\mathcal{C}
.
of a 2-category
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}^{\prime}
that we define now.

•

\nabla\sqcup{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}
(
\nabla

is trivial

m=\nabla

n=\nabla

Remark 5.2
.

The motivation for (
33
) follows our ansatz, Remark
4.1
, that in the representation on
\mathbf{TL}
, a box
\boxed{k}
should act as multiplication by the scalar
[n+k+1]/[n+k+2]
if
n+k\geq 0
. We assign the value zero to all other boxes so that
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}^{\prime}}(n,-)
is defined as a quotient of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
. In this way, no invertible box in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
is mapped to zero. This assignment of boxes to constants also eases the description of bases of endomorphism categories.

On the other hand, the bubble
{k}
in region
n
should act on
\mathbf{TL}
by projecting onto the
W^{n}_{n-2k}
isotypic component (see Appendix
A
for a discussion of these modules). If
n-2k<0
this module is 0. We therefore set such a morphism to 0 as well. Whereas the sum over these nonzero components is the identity on any module, the sum of nonzero bubbles is
1
. See also Remark
4.11
.
∎

For each
n\geq 0
, let
\mathbbm{1}_{n}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n)
denote the tensor unit of
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n)
and
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n})
its algebra of endomorphisms in
2\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n},\mathbbm{1}_{n})
. As a consequence of the construction of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
,
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n})
is described as the quotient of
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
by the relations (
31
)-(
33
).

Remark 5.3
.

For
n\geq 0
, let
G_{n}:\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n})
be the quotient map determined by the relations (
31
)-(
33
). By definition
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n})=\operatorname{im}(G_{n})
.
∎

Remark 5.4
.

24
) vanish if
n-2k+2=0

5.2.
Isomorphisms in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,m)

We discuss the isomorphisms which are introduced in the hom-categories
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,m)
in comparison to those of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
stated in Section
4.2
and how some isomorphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
become trivialized. The assignment of
\boxed{k}\overset{n}{=}\dfrac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}
for
n+k\geq 0
means that boxes appearing in relations are invertible, and can be used to construct isomorphisms which are not present in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. Relation (
31
) implies a number of diagrams which are
present in the defining relations of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
but
vanish in certain hom-categories of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
. Many of these follow from the basic relations

in

. At this critical value, boxes
\boxed{-2k-1}
which appear in the relevant relations are also mapped to zero and so the isomorphism fails in this case. If

, then both
C_{k}
and
C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}

and the isomorphism becomes trivial. The various isomorphisms dependent on the value of
n
relative to
k
are summarized in Table
1
.

Proposition 5.5
.

The isomorphisms in Table
1
hold in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,-)
.

\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\mbox{Above critical values}&\mbox{At critical values}&\mbox{Critical values}\\
\hline\cr C_{k}Q_{+}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\oplus C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k-1}&C_{k}Q_{+}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k-1}&n=2k-1\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k-1\\
\hline\cr Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\oplus C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}&Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}&n=2k\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k}Q_{-}\cong C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}\oplus C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k+1}&C_{k}Q_{-}\cong C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}&n=2k+1\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k+1\\
\hline\cr Q_{-}C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}\oplus C_{k-1}Q_{-}C_{k}&Q_{-}C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}&n=2k\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k}&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k-1}Q_{-}C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k-1}\cong C_{k-1}&\text{none}&n=2(k-1)\\
&0\cong 0&n<2(k-1)\\
\hline\cr C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}&\text{none}&n=2k\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k}\cong C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k-1}Q_{-}C_{k}&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}&\text{none}&n=2k\\
&0\cong 0&n<2k\\
\hline\cr C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k+1}Q_{-}C_{k+1}\cong C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k+1}&\text{none}&n=2(k+1)\\
&0\cong 0&n<2(k+1)\end{array}

Table 1.
“Generic” isomorphisms in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,-)
and their modification at critical values.

Proof.

The most interesting relation in the table is
C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}
, which we will prove directly for
n>2k
. The isomorphism
C_{k+1}Q_{-}C_{k}Q_{-}C_{k}\cong C_{k+1}Q_{-}C_{k+1}Q_{-}C_{k}
is a consequence of rotating the diagrams.
The proof of other relations in the table are straightforward to verify from Section
4.2
or the relations from (
17
), (
18
), (
23
), and Remark
4.2
with (
33
). For the critical values of
k
relative to
n
, certain morphisms will vanish because of (
31
) and (
33
).

To prove
C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}Q_{+}C_{k}\cong C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k+1}Q_{+}C_{k}
in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n+2)
for
n>2k
, we show that the maps

.

The proof of Proposition

.

Remark 5.7
.

In each isomorphism of Table

, if

, where

.

6.
Action of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
on
\mathbf{TL}

We recall the notion of a 2-categorical representation in the sense of
[
LS13
]
. Let
\mathcal{X}=\bigoplus_{m\in M}\mathcal{X}_{m}
be an
M
-graded additive category, where
M
is a monoid. The collection of endofunctors on
\mathcal{X}
naturally forms a 2-category whose objects are the elements of
M
, whose 1-morphisms from
n
to
m
, for
n,m\in M
, are the functors from
\mathcal{X}_{n}
to
\mathcal{X}_{m}
, and whose 2-morphisms are natural transformations. Denote such an endofunctor category by
\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{X})
. If
\mathcal{C}
is a category, then a functor
\rho:\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{X})
is called a
representation of
\mathcal{C}
on
\mathcal{X}
and we say that
\mathcal{C}
acts on
\mathcal{X}
. In this section, we construct a representation of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
on the category of Temperley-Lieb modules
\mathbf{TL}:=\bigoplus_{n\geq-1}\mathrm{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
, with the convention that
\operatorname{TL}_{-1}\mathrm{-mod}
is a null object denoted
\nabla
.

Every
(\operatorname{TL}_{m},\operatorname{TL}_{n})
-bimodule
M
determines a functor

(35)

\displaystyle M\otimes-:\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}\to\operatorname{TL}_{m}\mathrm{-mod}

\displaystyle V\mapsto M\otimes V

and any homomorphism
M_{1}\to M_{2}
of
(\operatorname{TL}_{m},\operatorname{TL}_{n})
-bimodules gives a natural
transformation between the corresponding functors. In this way, a representation of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
is an assignment of bimodule maps to diagrams.

For
k,l\leq n
, let
{}_{k}(n)_{l}
denote
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
as a
(\operatorname{TL}_{k},\operatorname{TL}_{l})
-bimodule. Tensoring the bimodules
{}_{n+1}(n+1)_{n}
and
{}_{n-1}(n)_{n}
correspond to induction and restriction functors on
\mathbf{TL}
, respectively.

We now propose a representation
\rho^{\prime}:\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}^{\prime}\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
which makes the following assignments.

•

On objects,
\rho^{\prime}(n)=n
for
n\geq 0
and
\rho^{\prime}(\nabla)=\nabla
.

•

The functor
\rho^{\prime}
maps the object 0 in each hom-category to 0. Each 1-morphism
Q_{\epsilon}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n+\|\epsilon\|)
with
\epsilon=\epsilon_{\ell}\dots\epsilon_{1}
is mapped by
\rho^{\prime}
to a sequence of induction and restriction bimodules, with
+
mapping to induction and
-
mapping to restriction.

•

On 2-morphisms,
\rho^{\prime}
makes the following assignments
6
6

6

We use a notational shorthand
[x\mapsto\ast]:X\to Y
to describe a function
f:X\to Y
defined by a formula
f(x)=\ast
.
on elementary diagrams

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\otimes y\mapsto xy\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n-1}(n)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n)_{n},

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto x\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n+1)_{n+1}(n+1)_{n},

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x)\right]:{}_{n}(n+1)_{n+1}(n+1)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n)_{n},

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,r\in P^{n}\\
p_{n}=r_{n}\end{subarray}}c_{r}e_{p,r}\otimes e_{r,p}x\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n}\mapsto{}_{n}(n)_{n-1}(n)_{n},

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto xe_{n+1}\right]:{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n}\to{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n},

where the map
x\mapsto\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x)
is the right partial trace of
x
as defined in (
4
) and
\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,r\in P^{n}\\
p_{n}=r_{n}\end{subarray}}c_{r}e_{p,r}\otimes e_{r,p}
is as described in Section
A.3
.

Remark 6.1
.

In a slight abuse of notation, we use
\overset{n}{=}
to denote an equality in a hom-category
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})}(n,-)
, when it is clear that we are considering an equality of morphisms under
\rho^{\prime}
. Its use here is similar to that in
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
where
\overset{n}{=}
indicates the rightmost region label on diagrams is
n
and establishes that the equality is between natural transformations of functors whose sources are
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. This convention fits with our ansatz in Remark
4.1
.

The notation
\overset{n}{=}
will typically be reserved for giving an explicit description of an action of a diagram on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. In addition, we will use
\overset{\bullet}{=}
if an equality
\overset{n}{=}
holds for all
n\geq 0
. Typically, this will be used for equalities between the images of diagrams under
\rho^{\prime}
.
∎

Since
\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
is idempotent complete, the proposed functor
\rho^{\prime}
extends to a functor
\rho:\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
. In Corollary
6.9
, each object
C_{k}
is shown to map to
P_{k}
, the functor which projects onto the
W^{n}_{n-2k}
isotypic component of any
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-module. Here
W^{n}_{n-2k}
is an irreducible
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
defined in Appendix
A
.

Theorem 6.2
.

The functor
\rho
is well-defined and determines a representation of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
on
\mathbf{TL}
.

It is sufficient to prove the claim for
\rho^{\prime}
by showing that the defining relations on 2-morphisms in
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
hold when interpreted as maps of Temperley-Lieb bimodules according to the assignments above. Therefore, the following corollary is a tautological consequence.

Corollary 6.3
.

The images of
Q_{+}
,
Q_{-}
, and
C_{k}
under
\rho
are consistent with the isomorphsisms described in Table
1
and Proposition
5.6
.

Remark 6.4
.

Corollary
6.3
can also be proven by explicitly computing the induction, restriction, and projection functors on simple modules in
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. For an irreducible
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
representation
W^{n}_{m}
, the functors
\operatorname{Ind}
,
\operatorname{Res}
, and
P_{k}
act as

(36)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Ind}(W^{n}_{m})

\displaystyle\cong W^{n+1}_{m+1}\oplus\overline{\delta}_{m,0}W^{n+1}_{m-1},

(37)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Res}(W^{n}_{m})

\displaystyle\cong\overline{\delta}_{m,n}W^{n-1}_{m+1}\oplus\overline{\delta}_{m,0}W^{n-1}_{m-1},

(38)

\displaystyle P_{k}(W^{n}_{m})

\displaystyle\cong\delta_{m,n-2k}W^{n}_{n-2k}

from Appendix
A.1
. We use the convention that
W^{n}_{m}=0
if
m<0
,
m>n
, or
m\not\equiv n\operatorname{mod}2
. We write
\overline{\delta}_{ij}\coloneq 1-\delta_{ij}
to emphasize these conventions and to avoid confusion when composing these functors. With this presentation of induction, restriction, and projection it is straightforward to verify the isomorphisms in Table
1
and Proposition
5.6
.

It is important to remark that an instance of “none” in the table corresponds to an instance where the generic isomorphism implies a relation between a zero and a nonzero object, as is the case in
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
. For example, if
n=2(k-1)
so that
n+1-2k=-1
, then

\displaystyle P_{k-1}(W^{n}_{0})\cong W^{n}_{0}\,,

\displaystyle P_{k-1}\circ\operatorname{Res}\circ P_{k}\circ\operatorname{Ind}\circ P_{k-1}(W^{n}_{0})\cong P_{k-1}\circ\operatorname{Res}\circ P_{k}(W^{n+1}_{1})\cong 0\,.

Hence, there is no isomorphism between
P_{k-1}
and
P_{k-1}\circ\operatorname{Res}\circ P_{k}\circ\operatorname{Ind}\circ P_{k-1}
.
∎

We begin the proof of Theorem
6.2
by noting that some relations were proven in
[
Qui17
]
, see Section
A.3
. These include the isotopy relation and the first relations in (
16
) and (
17
). We proceed by first investigating the action of diagrams which are generated only by Temperley-Lieb generators. In the representation, it is enough to show that the relations in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
hold for all choices of rightmost region labels
n\geq 0
. The proof of the theorem is complete once the image of all relations in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}
mapped to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,m)
and interpreted as equalities of bimodule maps (i.e. 2-morphisms in
\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
) are verified for all rightmost region labels (i.e. 2-objects in
\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
).

Fix
n\geq 1
. Then the left side of the above maps
x\otimes y\in{}_{n+2}(n+2){}_{n}(n+1)_{n}
to
xe^{\prime}_{n+1}ye^{\prime}_{n+1}=x\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(y)e^{\prime}_{n+1}
which is exactly the image of
x\otimes y
under the right morphism.

The second relation is proven directly for
n\geq 0
. The left side of the relation determines an endomorphism of the bimodule
{}_{n+1}(n+2)_{n}
, mapping
x
to
\operatorname{ptr}_{n+2}(xe^{\prime}_{n+1})e^{\prime}_{n+1}
. Using the Jones basis of the Temperley-Lieb algebra
[
RSA14
]
,
x=x_{1}+x_{2}e^{\prime}_{n+1}x_{3}
for some
x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\in\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}
. Then as

\displaystyle\operatorname{ptr}_{n+2}(xe^{\prime}_{n+1})e^{\prime}_{n+1}

\displaystyle=(x_{1}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+2}(e^{\prime}_{n+1})+x_{2}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+2}(e^{\prime}_{n+1}x_{3}e^{\prime}_{n+1}))e^{\prime}_{n+1}

\displaystyle=x_{1}e^{\prime}_{n+1}+x_{2}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+2}(\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x_{3}))e^{\prime}_{n+1}

\displaystyle=(x_{1}+x_{2}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x_{3}))e^{\prime}_{n+1}

\displaystyle=(x_{1}+x_{2}e^{\prime}_{n+1}x_{3})e^{\prime}_{n+1}=xe^{\prime}_{n+1}

the claim follows.
∎

.

6.2.
Action of Bubbles

Before discussing additional relations involving boxes, namely those in which boxes are introduced i.e. (
18
), (
17
), (
24
), and (
23
); we must first discuss the action of bubbles
{k}
beginning with the
0
labeled circle. The latter equality in (
16
) follows from our definition of
{0}
. Since
{0}
appears in the definition of both diagrams in (
10
) and are related to each other by (
12
), we compute both of their actions on
\mathbf{TL}
explicitly to show that
{0}
is well-defined. Quinn proved in
[
Qui17
, Prop. 5.2.5]
that the left diagram in (
10
) acts as an idempotent endomorphism of the induction bimodule (
89
). Indeed, we show that it acts as multiplication by the Jones-Wenzl idempotent
f^{(n+1)}
on

Expanding the path

in the sum, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq m\leq n}\sum_{p,r\in P^{n}_{m}}\frac{[r_{n-1}+1]}{[m+1]}\frac{1}{|P^{n-1}_{r_{n-1}}|}e_{p,r}e_{n}^{\prime}e_{p,r}

\displaystyle=\sum_{0<m\leq n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n}_{m}\\
r^{\prime}\in P^{n}_{m-1}\end{subarray}}\frac{[m]}{[m+1]}\frac{1}{|P^{n-1}_{m-1}|}v_{p}f^{(m)}e_{m}^{\prime}f^{(m)}\check{v}_{p}+\sum_{0\leq m<n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n}_{m}\\
r^{\prime}\in P^{n}_{m+1}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{|P^{n-1}_{m+1}|}v_{p}f^{(m+1)}\check{v}_{p}

\displaystyle=\sum_{0\leq m\leq n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n}_{m}\end{subarray}}v_{p}\left(\frac{[m]}{[m+1]}f^{(m)}e_{m}^{\prime}f^{(m)}+f^{(m+1)}\right)\check{v}_{p}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n}_{n}\end{subarray}}v_{p}f^{(n+1)}\check{v}_{p}

\displaystyle=\sum_{0\leq m\leq n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n}_{m}\end{subarray}}e_{p,p}-f^{(n+1)}

\displaystyle=1-f^{(n+1)}

Proof.

Consider
x\in{}_{n}({n+2})_{n}
. The image of
x
under the right morphism is
e_{n+1}xe_{n+1}
, which can be written as
e_{n+1}x^{\prime}
for some
x^{\prime}\in\operatorname{TL}_{n}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{TL}_{n+2}
using the Jones basis
[
RSA14
, Prop. 2.3]
. Applying the left morphism to
x
yields

\displaystyle x\mapsto e_{n+1}xe_{n+1}

\displaystyle\mapsto{\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+1}\circ{\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+2}(e_{n+1}xe_{n+1})\mapsto e_{n+1}\left({\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+1}\circ{\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+2}(e_{n+1}xe_{n+1})\right)e_{n+1}

\displaystyle=e_{n+1}\left({\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+1}\circ{\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+2}(e_{n+1}x^{\prime})\right)e_{n+1}=e_{n+1}\left({\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+1}\circ{\operatorname{ptr}}_{n+2}(e_{n+1})\right)x^{\prime}e_{n+1}

\displaystyle=e_{n+1}x^{\prime}e_{n+1}=e_{n+1}x^{\prime}=e_{n+1}xe_{n+1}.

Thus proving the identity.
∎

Corollary 6.9
.

Let
M
be a
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-module and recall that
C_{k}
is image of the idempotent
{k}
in
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
. Then
\rho(C_{k})(M)=P_{k}(M)
is the projection onto the
W^{n}_{n-2k}
isotypic component of
M
.

Proof.

We have already shown that
{0}
acts by
f^{(n)}
on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-modules, and therefore is the projection onto the trivial isotypic component
W^{n}_{n}
. Thus we proceed by induction and show that
{k}
acts as
\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{p,p}
on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. By Proposition
6.7
and Lemma

It is therefore enough to compute the action of the latter on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. As an endomorphism of
{}_{n+1}(n+1)_{n}
, it acts via multiplication by

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,r\in P^{n}\\
s\in P^{n-1}_{n-1-2k}\end{subarray}}\frac{[r_{n-1}+1]}{[r_{n}+1]}\frac{1}{|P^{n-1}_{r_{n}-1}|}e_{p,r}e_{s,s}e_{n}^{\prime}e_{r,p}

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\frac{[n-2k]}{[n+1-2k]}v_{p}e_{n}^{\prime}\check{v}_{p}+\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2-2k}}v_{p}f^{(n-1-2k)}\check{v}_{p}

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in P^{n+1}_{n-1-2k}}e_{p,p}=\sum_{p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2(k+1)}}e_{p,p}

The second equality follows from Remark
A.1
and the claim is proven.
∎

Proof.

For a given
n\geq 0
, the action of the clockwise nested circle is multiplication by

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,r\in P^{n}\\
p_{n}=r_{n}\end{subarray}}\sum_{s\in P^{n-1}_{n-1-2k}}\frac{[p_{n-1}+1]}{[p_{n}+1]}\frac{1}{|P^{n-1}_{p_{n-1}}|}e_{p,r}e_{s,s}e_{r,p}=\sum_{p,r\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\frac{[n-2k]}{[n-2k+1]}e_{p,p}+\sum_{p,r\in P^{n}_{n-2-2k}}\frac{[n-2k]}{[n-2k-1]}e_{p,p}\,.

This agrees with the proposed equality, including the cases
n-1-2k<0
.
For the counterclockwise circle, it acts as multiplication by

\displaystyle\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}\left(\sum_{p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}e_{p,p}\right)

\displaystyle=\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}\left(\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}v_{p}f^{(n+1)}\check{v}_{p}+\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n+2-2k}}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+3]}v_{p}e_{n}\check{v}_{p}\right)

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+1]}e_{p,p}+\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n+2-2k}}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+3]}e_{p,p}

as desired.
∎

Equation (
32
) together with Lemma
6.10
imply that the relations for the unnested circles in (
17
) and (
18
) hold. See also Remark
4.11
.

Proof.

The left side of the equality acting on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
is the endomorphism of
{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n}
given via multiplication by

\displaystyle\sum_{p,r\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}e_{p,p}e_{n+1}^{\prime}e_{r,r}

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}v_{p}f^{(n+1-2k)}e_{n+1}^{\prime}f^{(n+1-2k)}\check{v}_{p}+\sum_{p,r\in P^{n}_{n+2-2k}}\left(\frac{[n+2-2k]}{[n+3-2k]}\right)^{2}v_{p}\cup_{n+2-2k}f^{(n+2-2k)}\cap_{n+2-2k}\check{v}_{p}\,.

The resulting expression is equivalent to that obtained from the right side of the equality.
∎

Proof.

Since these relations are mirror images of each other across a horizontal axis, their proofs are also related by reversing the order of multiplication. Therefore, we only write the computation for the first relation. The left side of the equality acting on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
is the endomorphism of
{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n}
multiply by

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2(k+1)}\\
r\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}\end{subarray}}e_{p,p}e_{n+1}^{\prime}e_{r,r}=\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\frac{[n-2k]}{[n+1-2k]}v_{p}e^{\prime}_{n-2k}e^{\prime}_{n+1-2k}f^{(n+1-2k)}\check{v}_{p}

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\frac{[n-2k]}{[n+1-2k]}v_{p}e^{\prime}_{n-2k}\check{v}_{p}e^{\prime}_{n+1-2k}-\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}\left(\frac{[n-2k]}{[n+1-2k]}\right)^{2}v_{p}\cup_{n-2k}f^{(n-2k)}\cap_{n-2k}\check{v}_{p}\,.

This is the same expression obtained from the right side of the equality.
∎

Proof.

Fix
n\geq 0
and let
x\in{}_{n}(n+1)_{n}
. If
n+1-2k<0
, then both claims follow from (
31
) as each diagram is the zero morphism. We prove the first claim, and the other is proven similarly. The left side of the proposed equality maps
x
to

\displaystyle\sum_{r\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{r,r}\cdot x\cdot\sum_{p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}e_{p,p}\sum_{s\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{s,s}=\sum_{r\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{r,r}\sum_{t,p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}x^{t}_{p}e_{t,p}\sum_{s\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{s,s}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t,p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}\\
t_{n-1}=p_{n-1}=n-2k\end{subarray}}x^{t}_{p}e_{t,p}

where coefficients
x_{p}^{t}\in{\mathbb{C}}(q)
satisfy
xv_{p}=\sum_{t\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}x^{t}_{p}v_{t}
for all
p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}
.

Whereas on the right side,
x
maps to

\displaystyle\frac{[n-2k+1]}{[n-2k+2]}\sum_{r\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{r,r}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}\left(x\cdot\sum_{p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}e_{p,p}\right)\sum_{s\in P^{n}_{n+1-2k}}e_{s,s}

\displaystyle=\frac{[n-2k+1]}{[n-2k+2]}\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}\left(\sum_{r\in P^{n}_{n-2k}}e_{r,r}\sum_{t,p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}}x^{t}_{p}e_{t,p}\right)\sum_{s\in P^{n}_{n+1-2k}}e_{s,s}

\displaystyle=\frac{[n-2k+1]}{[n-2k+2]}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t,p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}\\
t_{n-1}=p_{n-1}=n-2k\end{subarray}}x^{t}_{p}\frac{[n+2-2k]}{[n+1-2k]}e_{t^{\prime},p^{\prime}}\sum_{s\in P^{n}_{n+1-2k}}e_{s,s}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t,p\in P^{n+1}_{n+1-2k}\\
t_{n-1}=p_{n-1}=n-2k\end{subarray}}x^{t}_{p}e_{t,p}

Thus, equality holds.
∎

7.
Basis Statements

We describe bases for
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
and certain subalgebras of morphism spaces of
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,-)
. The arguments for proving these results rely on the action of
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
on
\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{TL})
.

7.1.
The Box Algebra

We first describe the subalgebras generated by boxes. This discussion is relevant for understanding a basis of the subalgebra generated by boxes in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
. It does not apply to
\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}
where boxes have been identified with scalars.

Definition 7.1
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
denote the unital commutative algebra over
\mathbb{C}(q)
with generators
b_{k}
for
k\geq 0
and relations
b_{k+1}b_{k}=[2]b_{k+1}-1
. We call
\mathcal{B}
the
box algebra
.

Introduce the notation

b_{[k;m]}=b_{k}b_{k-1}\cdots b_{k-m}\in\mathcal{B}

for
k\geq 0
and
0\leq m\leq k
. Recall that nonnegative quantum integers may be defined recursively by

(43)

\displaystyle[m]=[2][m-1]-[m-2]

with
[1]=1
and
[0]=0
, and where
[2]=q+q^{-1}
.

Lemma 7.2
.

Fix
k\geq 0
, and
0\leq m\leq k
. Then the equality

\displaystyle b_{[k;m]}=[m+1]b_{k}-[m]

holds in
\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

We give a proof by induction on
m
for any given
k\geq 0
. We can easily see that the case
m=0
holds. Assume that the lemma holds for all pairs
k^{\prime},m\in{\mathbb{Z}}
such that
0\leq k^{\prime}\leq k
and
0\leq m<k^{\prime}
. Fix
m
with
0\leq m<k
. Then
b_{[k;m+1]}=b_{k}b_{[k-1;m]}
. Since
b_{k}b_{k-1}=[2]b_{k}-1
, the claim now follows by induction:

\displaystyle b_{[k;m+1]}

\displaystyle=b_{k}b_{[k-1;m]}=b_{k}([m+1]b_{k-1}-[m])=[m+1]([2]b_{k}-1)-[m]b_{k}=[m+2]b_{k}-[m+1].\qed

Lemma 7.3
.

Fix
k\geq 0
, and
0<m\leq k
. Then the equality

\displaystyle b_{k}b_{k-m}=\dfrac{1}{[m]}\left([m+1]b_{k}+[m-1]b_{k-m}-[m]\right).

holds in
\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
7.2
,

[m+1]b_{k}-[m]=b_{[k;m]}=b_{[k;m-1]}b_{k-m}=([m]b_{k}-[m-1])b_{k-m}\,.

The claim follows by expanding the above and isolating
b_{k}b_{k-m}
.
∎

Lemma 7.4
.

Let
m>-1
and
p\geq 0
be integers. Then

\displaystyle\left(\frac{[m]}{[m+1]}\right)^{p}=q^{p}(1-q^{2m})^{p}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{i+p-1\choose p-1}q^{2i(m+1)}\,.

Proof.

Write

\displaystyle\frac{[m]}{[m+1]}=\frac{q^{m}-q^{-m}}{q^{m+1}-q^{-(m+1)}}=\frac{q(q^{2m}-1)}{q^{2(m+1)}-1}=q(1-q^{2m})\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}q^{2i(m+1)}.

Recall that the exponentiation of a geometric series is given by the series
\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}r^{i}\right)^{p}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{i+p-1\choose p-1}r^{i}
. The desired formula now follows by taking
r=q^{2(m+1)}
.
∎

For any integers
n
and
k
such that
n+k+2>0
, the identity

(44)

\displaystyle\frac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}\cdot\frac{[n+k]}{[n+k+1]}=\frac{[n+k]}{[n+k+2]}=\frac{[2][n+k+1]-[n+k+2]}{[n+k+2]}=[2]\frac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}-1

holds. Thus, for
n\geq-1
, there are algebra homomorphisms

(45)

\displaystyle\varrho_{n}:\mathcal{B}

\displaystyle\to{\mathbb{C}}(q)

\displaystyle b_{k}

\displaystyle\mapsto\frac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}

Observe that if
n\geq 0
, then no generator is mapped to zero. However, this map is not an injection for any
n
.

Proposition 7.5
.

There is a basis of
\mathcal{B}
over
\mathbb{C}(q)
spanned by

\displaystyle\{1\}\cup\left\{b_{k}^{p}:k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},p\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\right\}.

Proof.

We determine that
\{1\}\cup\left\{b_{k}^{p}:k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},p\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\right\}
is a spanning set by Lemma
7.3
, which shows the product of any two distinct
b_{k}
and
b_{l}
can be expressed as a
\mathbb{C}(q)
-linear combination of
b_{k}
,
b_{l}
, and
1
.

To prove this spanning set is a basis, suppose there is a linear dependence
\sum_{k,p}a_{k,p}b_{k}^{p}=0
, where all but finitely many
a_{k,p}\in\mathbb{C}(q)
are nonzero. Assume all
a_{k,p}\in{\mathbb{C}}[q]
by first clearing denominators then multiplying by some power of
q
. Let
a_{0,0}
denote the coefficient of
1\in\mathcal{B}
.
The image of this relation under
\varrho_{n}
as in (
45
) implies
\sum_{k,p}a_{k,p}\left(\frac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}\right)^{p}=0
for all
n>-2
.

By Lemma
7.4
, this relation becomes

\displaystyle\sum_{k,p}a_{k,p}q^{p}(1-q^{2(n+k+1)})^{p}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{i+p-1\choose p-1}q^{2i(n+k+2)}=0\,.

Set
a^{\prime}_{k,p}=a_{k,p}q^{p}
and
x=x(n)=q^{2n}
. Thus,

\displaystyle\sum_{k,p}a^{\prime}_{k,p}(1-xq^{2(k+1))})^{p}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{i+p-1\choose p-1}q^{2i(k+2)}x^{i}=0\,.

In this way, the coefficient of
x^{j}
must be zero for all
j\geq 0
. We compute

\displaystyle y_{k,p}(x,q):=(1-xq^{2(k+1))})^{p}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{i+p-1\choose p-1}q^{2i(k+2)}x^{i}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{p}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{i}{p\choose j}{i-j+p-1\choose i-j}q^{2(i-j)}\right)q^{2i(k+1)}x^{i}+\sum_{i=p+1}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{p}{p\choose j}{i-j+p-1\choose i-j}q^{2(i-j)}\right)q^{2i(k+1)}x^{i}\,.

Let
P
(and
K
) be the maximum value of
p
(and
k
) among all nonzero
a^{\prime}_{k,p}
in the relation. Set
L=\max_{k,p}(\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{k,p}))
and
\ell=\max_{p}(\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{K,p}))
.

For a given
k
and
p
, the coefficient of
x^{i}
in the power series
y_{k,p}(x,q)
is a
{\mathbb{C}}
-linear combination of
q^{2i(k+2)},q^{2i(k+2)-2},\dots,q^{2i(k+2)-2p}
. For each
i
, suppose that these exists
k\neq K
and
j,p
such that
\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{k,p}q^{2i(k+2)-2j})\geq\deg_{q}(q^{\ell+2i(K+2)})=\ell+2i(K+2)
. In which case
\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{k,p}q^{-2j-\ell})\geq 2i(K-k)\geq 2i
. Since
\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{k,p}q^{-2j-\ell})
is independent of
i
and is at most
L
, our above supposition fails for
i>L
. Thus, only terms in the expansion of some
a^{\prime}_{K,p^{\prime}}y_{K,p^{\prime}}
can cancel the
q^{\ell+2i(K+2)}x^{i}
term in
a^{\prime}_{K,p}y_{K,p}
.

As
\deg_{q}(a^{\prime}_{K,p})\leq\ell
for all
p
, let
\hat{a}_{p}
be the coefficient of
q^{\ell}
in
a^{\prime}_{K,p}
for each
p
. Comparing coefficients of
q^{\ell+2i(K+2)}x^{i}
in the relation, i.e.
k=K
and
j=0
, we determine
\sum_{p}\hat{a}_{p}{i+p-1\choose i}=0
for all
i>L
.

Let
\hat{P}
be the largest
p
such that
\hat{a}_{p}
is nonzero. Consider
i=L+\hat{P}
. By the binomial coefficient identity
{i+j\choose i}={i+j-1\choose i}+{i+j-1\choose i-1}
, we have

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\leq\hat{P}}\hat{a}_{p}{(L+\hat{P})+p-1\choose L+\hat{P}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\leq\hat{P}}\hat{a}_{p}{(L+\hat{P})+p-2\choose L+\hat{P}}+\cancel{\sum_{p\leq\hat{P}}\hat{a}_{p}{(L+\hat{P}-1)+p-1\choose L+\hat{P}-1}}

and iterating on this

\displaystyle 0=\sum_{p\leq\hat{P}}\hat{a}_{p}{(L+\hat{P})+p-\hat{P}\choose L+\hat{P}}=\sum_{p\leq\hat{P}}\hat{a}_{p}{L+p\choose L+\hat{P}}=\hat{a}_{\hat{P}}.

Thus, we have reached a contradiction as we have assumed
\hat{a}_{\hat{P}}\neq 0
. Hence there are no relations among the proposed basis elements.
∎

Proposition 7.6
.

The map
\psi_{0,\mathcal{B}}:\mathcal{B}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
which sends
b_{k}
to the box labeled
k
is an injection.

Proof.

Suppose that
\psi_{0,\mathcal{B}}(\sum_{k,p}a_{k,p}b_{k}^{p})=0
, where all but finitely many
a_{k,p}\in\mathbb{C}(q)
are nonzero.
For each
n\geq 0
recall the homomorphisms
G_{n}:\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})\to 2\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n)
defined in Remark
5.3
. Recall the maps
\varrho
and
\rho
defined in (
45
) and preceding Theorem
6.2
respectively. Let
\rho_{n}
be the restriction of
\rho
to
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
with target
\operatorname{End}(\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod})
. There is a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{C}}(q)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{End}(\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{0,\mathcal{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varrho_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{n}\circ G_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\times}

that maps
b_{k}
to the endomorphism which multiplies by
\frac{[n+k+1]}{[n+k+2]}
. As shown in Proposition
7.5
, the collection of maps
\varrho_{n}
distinguishes all elements of
\mathcal{B}
. That is, for all
b\in\mathcal{B}
such that
b\neq 0
, then there exists
n
such that
\varrho_{n}(b)\neq 0
. Thus, all
a_{k,p}
are zero and therefore
\psi_{0,\mathcal{B}}
is an injection.
∎

7.2.
Endomorphism Algebras

We give a description of
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
and
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(Q^{\otimes s}_{+,n})
as algebras.

Definition 7.7
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
denote the commutative algebra of orthogonal idempotents
\langle c_{0},c_{1},\dots\mid c_{k}c_{l}=\delta_{kl}c_{k}\rangle
over
\mathbb{C}(q)
. Let
\mathcal{C}_{n}
be the subquotient generated by
c_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor}
with the additional relation
1=c_{0}+c_{1}+\dots+c_{\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor}
.

Proposition 7.8
.

The natural map
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}:\mathcal{C}_{n}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(\mathbbm{1}_{n})
is an injection.

Proof.

To prove that
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}
is injective, assume that
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}(\sum_{k}a_{k}c_{k})=0
where each
a_{k}\in\mathbb{C}(q)
. Since
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}
is a homomorphism to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,n)
, we consider the composition of
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}
with
\rho_{n}
. Then each
c_{k}
acts as the projection onto the isotypic component of type
W^{n}_{n-2k}
according to Corollary
6.9
. Since
k\leq\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor
, the generators
c_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor}
act by nonzero projections onto distinct simple summands. Therefore, they act linearly independently on the direct sum of modules
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor}W^{n}_{n-2i}
. It now follows that the coefficients
a_{k}
must all be zero.
∎

Corollary 7.9
.

Let
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
be the map which sends
c_{k}
to the bubble labeled
k
. Then
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C}}
is an injection.

Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Proposition
7.8
. By composing
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C}}
with
\rho_{K}\circ G_{K}
, with
G_{K}
as defined in Remark
5.3
, for
K
sufficiently large, the generators
c_{k}
act linearly independently on the
\operatorname{TL}_{K}
-module
\bigoplus^{\left\lfloor K/2\right\rfloor}_{k=0}W^{K}_{K-2k}
.
∎

Proposition 7.10
.

The map
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}
is an isomorphism.

Proof.

It remains to show that
\psi_{0,\mathcal{C},n}
is a surjection. Any endomorphism of
\mathbbm{1}_{n}
is a
{\mathbb{C}}(q)
-linear combination of products of bubbles
{k}
and oriented trivalent graphs without boundary points. Each edge of each graph is either solid or doubled, and each vertex joins two solid segments with the same orientation and one doubled segment with the opposite orientation. Here orientation means outward or inward with respect to the vertex. Each region in the complement of a graph contains at most one bubble
{k}
by (
21
).

Notice that each connected component of a solid (non-doubled strand) in a graph is a closed curve with an even number of vertices (possibly zero). Consider such a component which also contains no solid curves in the region it bounds. Resolve any closed doubled curves on its interior according to Lemma
4.9
and evaluate any resulting boxes according to (
33
). If the solid curve has any doubled segments on its interior, consider a region bounded by the solid curve and a doubled edge which has no other doubled edges on its interior. There may be an even number of vertices on the boundary of this region, at each such vertex there is a doubled segment on the exterior of the region. These vertices may be removed in pairs using (
15
). Now apply (
16
), and Lemma
4.8
if necessary, to reduce the number of doubled edges in the region bounded by the solid curve. Repeat until there are no such edges remaining. Relation (
15
) may be applied to remove any remaining pairs of exterior doubled edges from the solid closed curve. The solid curve has been reduced to a
{\mathbb{C}}(q)
multiple of an oriented circle, which can be further simplified using (
17
) and (
18
).

Apply the above to remove all solid curves from the graph. The resulting diagram may contain closed doubled curves which can be simplified using (
20
). The resulting diagram is now a linear combination of products of bubbles. Products may be simplified using (
21
), by (
31
) only bubbles with sufficiently small index are nonzero, and by (
32
) sums of bubbles may be simplified to
1
. Thus,
\psi_{0}
is a surjection.
∎

Corollary 7.11
.

The map
\psi_{0,\mathcal{B}}\otimes\psi_{0,\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(\mathbbm{1})
is an isomorphism of commutative algebras.

Proof.

The proof is identical to that of Proposition
7.10
with the exception that boxes are not evaluated as constants, but are instead moved to the unbounded region of any given diagram using (
21
).
∎

Definition 7.12
.

For
n>0
, write
\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
to denote the unital commutative algebra generated by
c_{i,j}
for
0\leq i\leq\left\lfloor(n+j)/2\right\rfloor
and
0\leq j\leq s
with relations

(46)

\displaystyle c_{i,j}c_{l,j}

\displaystyle=\delta_{il}c_{i,j},

\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor(n+j)/2\right\rfloor}c_{i,j}

\displaystyle=1

(47)

\displaystyle\delta_{j>0}c_{i,j}

\displaystyle=c_{i,j}(c_{i,j-1}+c_{i-1,j-1}),

\displaystyle\delta_{j<s}c_{i,j}

\displaystyle=(c_{i,j+1}+c_{i+1,j+1})c_{i,j}

where
c_{i,j}
is assumed to be zero if
i<0
or
i>\left\lfloor(n+j)/2\right\rfloor
.

For each
0\leq j\leq s
, there is an inclusion of
\mathcal{C}_{n+j}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
which maps the generator
c_{i}
to
c_{i,j}
. Indeed this map is an inclusion, as

c_{i,j}=\prod_{k=-j}^{s-j}c_{i+k,j+k}+(\text{terms with some factor $c_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}$ where each $|i^{\prime}-j^{\prime}|<|i-j|$})\,.

In this way we may present
\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
as
\mathcal{C}_{n+s}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\otimes\mathcal{C}_{n}
together with the relations in (
47
).

Lemma 7.13
.

A basis of
\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
given by sequences

\displaystyle\{c_{\boldsymbol{k}}=c_{k_{s},s}\cdots c_{k_{1},1}c_{k_{0},0}:0\leq k_{j}\leq\left\lfloor(n+j)/2\right\rfloor,k_{j+1}\in\{k_{j},k_{j}+1\}\}.

For example, for
0\leq i\leq\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor
we may express
c_{i,0}c_{i,2}\in\mathcal{C}_{n,3}
in this basis as

\displaystyle c_{i,0}c_{i,2}

\displaystyle=c_{i,2}c_{i,0}=\left[(c_{i+1,3}+c_{i,3})c_{i,2}(c_{i,1}+c_{i-1,1})\right]\left[(c_{i+1,1}+c_{i,1})c_{i,0}\right]=(c_{i+1,3}+c_{i,3})c_{i,2}c_{i,1}c_{i,0}

\displaystyle=c_{i+1,3}c_{i,2}c_{i,1}c_{i,0}+c_{i,3}c_{i,2}c_{i,1}c_{i,0},

where in the second equality we applied the relations (
47
).

Definition 7.14
.

Let
\operatorname{TL}^{+}_{s}(n)
be a
\mathbb{C}(q)
-algebra with generators
e^{\prime}_{j}
and
c_{k,i}
for
1\leq j\leq s-1
,
0\leq k\leq\left\lfloor(n+j)/2\right\rfloor
, and
0\leq i\leq s
. Each respective set of generators is subject to relations such that they generate
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
and
\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
as subalgebras. The other defining relations are:

(48)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}_{j}c_{k,i}

\displaystyle=c_{k,i}e^{\prime}_{j},

for
i\neq j

(49)

\displaystyle c_{k,j-1}e^{\prime}_{j}

\displaystyle=c_{k+1,j+1}c_{k,j-1}e^{\prime}_{j}=c_{k+1,j+1}e^{\prime}_{j},

(50)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}

\displaystyle=c_{k+1,i+1}c_{k+1,i}c_{k,i-1}\left(e^{\prime}_{i}-\frac{[n-2k]}{[n-2k+1]}\right)+c_{k,i+1}c_{k-1,i}c_{k-1,i-1}\left(e^{\prime}_{i}-\frac{[n-2k+4]}{[n-2k+3]}\right)

\displaystyle\phantom{=}+c_{k+1,i+1}c_{k,i}c_{k,i-1}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+1]}+c_{k,i+1}c_{k,i}c_{k-1,i-1}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+3]}.

The relation

(51)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}e^{\prime}_{i}

\displaystyle=\left(c_{k-1,i-1}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+3]}+c_{k,i-1}\frac{[n-2k+2]}{[n-2k+1]}\right)e^{\prime}_{i}

is readily verified using (
50
),

c_{k+1,i+1}(c_{k+1,i}+c_{k,i})c_{k,i-1}=c_{k+1,i+1}c_{k,i-1}
,
and
(e^{\prime}_{i})^{2}=[2]e^{\prime}_{i}
.

The Jones basis of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
for nonidentity elements consists of words

(52)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{jk}}=(e^{\prime}_{j_{1}}e^{\prime}_{j_{1}+1}\cdots e^{\prime}_{k_{1}})(e^{\prime}_{j_{2}}e^{\prime}_{j_{2}+1}\cdots e^{\prime}_{k_{2}})\cdots(e^{\prime}_{j_{r}}e^{\prime}_{j_{r}+1}\cdots e^{\prime}_{k_{r}})

where
s>j_{1}>j_{2}>\cdots>j_{r}>0
and
s>k_{1}>k_{2}>\cdots>k_{r}>0

[
RSA14
, Prop. 2.3]
. We write the identity element as
e^{\prime}_{00}
.

Proposition 7.15
.

There is a basis of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}^{+}(n)
consisting of products
c_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}
where
c_{\boldsymbol{k}}
is a basis vector of
\mathcal{C}_{n,s}
as in Lemma
7.13
and
e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}
is a basis vector of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
as in (
52
) with the additional constraints:

•

if
e^{\prime}_{\ell}e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}=[2]e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}
, then
\boldsymbol{k}_{\ell+1}=\boldsymbol{k}_{\ell-1}+1
,

•

if
n+j-2i=0
and
c_{i+1,j+2}c_{i,j+1}c_{i,j}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}=c_{\boldsymbol{k}}
, then
e^{\prime}_{j+1}e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}\neq[2]e^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{ij}}
.

Proof.

The defining relations in
\operatorname{TL}_{s}^{+}
give a rule to present any element of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}^{+}
in the desired form. The additional constraints are due to (
49
) and the exceptional form of (
50
), see also Remark
5.4
. It remains to show that any ambiguities in applying these rules can be resolved in the sense of Bergman’s diamond lemma
[
Ber78
]
. The ambiguities arising from relations which relate one monomial to another are easily resolved. Ambiguities for the relation involving
e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}
, namely the confluence conditions for
(e^{\prime}_{i})^{2}c_{k,i}
,
e^{\prime}_{i}e^{\prime}_{i\pm 1}e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}
,
e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}^{2}
, and
e^{\prime}_{i}c_{k,i}(c_{k,i\pm 1}+c_{k\pm 1,i\pm 1})
are resolved by short computations.
∎

Proposition 7.16
.

The map
\psi_{s,n}
is a surjection.

Proof.

Any diagram in
\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(Q_{+,n}^{\otimes s})
can be reduced to a diagram in a standard form. Any closed subgraph in a diagram may be simplified to a linear combination of bubbles by Proposition
7.10
. A bubble that appears directly below a disoriented cupcap may be moved above it and have the cupcap resolve according to (
24
). The result is a linear combination of Temperley-Lieb diagrams with at most one bubble in each region across the top of the complement of the diagram (including its sides). If there are no bubbles in these regions, we introduce a sum of bubbles into the rightmost region (any region is fine) using (
32
). We then use (
19
) to guarantee that each region across the top of the complement of the diagrams has a bubble. It is now easy to determine an element of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}^{+}(n)
which maps to this linear combination of diagrams.
∎

Conjecture 7.17
.

The map
\psi_{s,n}
is an injection.

Proving that
\psi_{s,n}
is injective is equivalent to showing that its kernel is generated by the relations of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}^{+}(n)
given in Definition
7.14
. This proof requires studying the action of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
on
Q_{+}^{\otimes s}
, which we discuss briefly in the next section.

7.3.
Action of
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
on

It follows from the first relation in (
15
) that the identification of idempotent Temperley-Lieb generators

with the disoriented cupcap over strands

and
i+1
(numbered right to left) defines a homomorphism
\operatorname{TL}_{s}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(Q_{+}^{\otimes s})
. Similarly, by rotating diagrams there is a homomorphism
\operatorname{TL}_{s}\to\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}}(Q_{-}^{\otimes s})
.

Now each idempotent in
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
defines an object in the idempotent complete category

. These include the projections onto irreducible representations discussed in Section

, among which the Jones-Wenzl idempotent

is a special case. The simplest of these idempotents and their complements are

.

The action of
e_{1}\in\operatorname{TL}_{2}
on
Q_{+,n}^{\otimes 2}C_{k}
determines an endomorphism of
\operatorname{Ind}^{2}(W^{n}_{m})
under
\rho
, namely multiply by
e_{n+2}
. Under this action, both the first and last summands vanish as capping a Jones-Wenzl idempotent yields zero and
vf^{(m)}=v\in W^{n}_{m}
. This observation is consistent with the relation in Lemma
4.8
, which implies a projection onto the
W^{n+2}_{n+2-2(k+1)}=W^{n+2}_{n-2k}
isotypic component. The images of these vectors are both nonzero multiples of

(57)

x
v
x
f^{(m)}

Note that the complement
1-e_{1}
of this idempotent endomorphism on
Q_{+,n}^{\otimes 2}
does not act as a projection onto the complementary summands
W^{n+2}_{n+2-2k}\oplus W^{n+2}_{n-2-2k}
. This is because
1-e_{n+2}
is nonzero on the
W^{n+2}_{n-2k}
summands of
\operatorname{Ind}^{2}(W^{n}_{n-2k})
. Further investigation of the interaction between the images of idempotents in
\operatorname{TL}_{s}
under
\rho
and the idempotents
C_{k}
requires a more careful treatment.

Remark 7.18
.

The affine Temperley-Lieb algebra also acts on
Q_{+}^{\otimes s}
. In future work, we use this action to compute
\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}})
.
