Given that
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
is a quotient of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}
, the isomorphisms given in Section
4.2
hold. Moreover, the “Above critical values” (large
n
) isomorphisms in Table
1
hold in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
. Indeed, no bubbles or boxes vanish among the morphisms witnessing the isomorphisms on objects given in the table. It is in this sense that we may also consider
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
a
n\to\infty
version of the categories
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,m)
.

Proposition 8.2
.

The isomorphisms in Section
4.2
and the large
n
relations in
5.2
hold in the full subcategory of
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
generated by
Q_{+}
,
Q_{-}
, and
C_{k}
for
k\geq 0
.

8.1.
Grothendieck Ring

Recall that the Grothendieck group of an additive category
\mathcal{C}
is abelian group
K_{0}(\mathcal{C})
with generators
X
for
X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})
and relations
[Z]=[X]+[Y]
whenever
Z\cong X\oplus Y
. The Grothendieck group is endowed with the structure of a ring with multiplication defined such that
[X][Y]=[X\otimes Y]
.

Definition 8.3
.

Let
\mathcal{K}
be the algebra generated by
x
,
y
and
c_{k}
for
k\geq 0
with relations

(59)

\displaystyle yx

\displaystyle=xy+c_{0}

\displaystyle c_{k}c_{\ell}

\displaystyle=\delta_{k\ell}c_{k}

(60)

\displaystyle c_{k}x~

\displaystyle=c_{k}x(c_{k}+c_{k-1})

\displaystyle xc_{k}~

\displaystyle=(c_{k}+c_{k+1})xc_{k}

(61)

\displaystyle c_{k}y~

\displaystyle=c_{k}y(c_{k}+c_{k+1})

\displaystyle yc_{k}~

\displaystyle=(c_{k}+c_{k-1})yc_{k}

(62)

\displaystyle c_{k+1}xc_{k}xc_{k}

\displaystyle=c_{k+1}xc_{k+1}xc_{k}

\displaystyle c_{k}yc_{k+1}yc_{k+1}

\displaystyle=c_{k}yc_{k}yc_{k+1}

(63)

\displaystyle c_{k}yc_{k}xc_{k}

\displaystyle=c_{k}

\displaystyle c_{k-1}yc_{k}xc_{k-1}

\displaystyle=c_{k-1}

(64)

\displaystyle c_{k}xc_{k}yc_{k}

\displaystyle=c_{k}

\displaystyle c_{k}xc_{k-1}yc_{k}

\displaystyle=c_{k}

(65)

\displaystyle yc_{k}x~

\displaystyle=c_{k}+c_{k-1}+c_{k}xyc_{k-1}+c_{k-1}xyc_{k}

\displaystyle xc_{k}y~

\displaystyle=c_{k}+c_{k+1}+c_{k}xyc_{k+1}+c_{k+1}xyc_{k}

(66)

\displaystyle c_{-1}

\displaystyle=0

\displaystyle yc_{0}x~

\displaystyle=c_{0}

The relations of
\mathcal{K}
are determined from the image of the isomorphisms in Proposition
8.2
under the
K_{0}
functor. We expect these to be a complete set of relations between the classes of these objects in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
, see Conjecture
8.5
.

We do not claim that
[Q_{+}]
,
[Q_{-}]
, and
[C_{k}]
form a complete set of generators for
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})
. For example, the Jones-Wenzl idempotents which act on
Q_{+}^{s}
, determine objects in
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
and therefore generators of
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})
, see Section
7.3
. However, we do not consider them here.

Proposition 8.4
.

Let
{K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})}^{\prime}
be the subalgebra of
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})
generated by
[Q_{+}]
,
[Q_{-}]
, and
[C_{k}]
. The homomorphism
\mathcal{K}\to{K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})}^{\prime}
determined by
x\mapsto[Q_{+}]
,
y\mapsto[Q_{-}]
,
c_{k}\mapsto[C_{k}]
is well-defined.

Conjecture 8.5
.

The map defined in Proposition
8.4
is an isomorphism.

Remark 8.6
.

We expect that there is a categorical version of “asymptotic representation” which applies to
\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty}
acting asymptotically on
\mathbf{TL}
, the notion is defined here for algebras and vector spaces in Definition
8.8
. Such an action would imply
K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})
acts on
K_{0}(\mathbf{TL})
. Mapping
\mathcal{K}
to
{K_{0}(\operatorname{\mathbf{W}}^{\infty})}^{\prime}
and applying the argument of Lemma
8.14
would prove Conjecture
8.5
.
∎

8.2.
Asymptotic Action

Assign a degree to each of the generators of
\mathcal{K}
,
\deg(x)=\deg(y)=1
and
\deg(c_{k})=0
for all
k\geq 0
. For
a,b\in\mathcal{K}
, set
\deg(a\cdot b)=\deg(a)+\deg(b)
. We filter
\mathcal{K}
by vector subspaces according to this degree, defining
\mathcal{K}_{n}=\{a\in\mathcal{K}|\deg(a)\leq n\}
.

Recall that
\mathbf{TL}
is the direct sum over
n
of
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. Then
\mathcal{T\!L}\coloneq K_{0}(\mathbf{TL})
is the abelian group with generators the classes of simple modules
\{[W^{n}_{m}]:0\leq m\leq n,m\equiv n\operatorname{mod}2\}
. By Remark
6.4
, the functors
\operatorname{Ind}
,
\operatorname{Res}
, and
P_{k}
determine endomorphisms of
\mathcal{T\!L}
:

(67)

\displaystyle[\operatorname{Ind}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]

\displaystyle=[W^{n+1}_{m+1}]+[W^{n+1}_{m-1}]

(68)

\displaystyle[\operatorname{Res}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]

\displaystyle=[W^{n-1}_{m+1}]+[W^{n-1}_{m-1}]

(69)

\displaystyle[P_{k}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]

\displaystyle=\delta_{m,n-2k}[W^{n}_{m}]

with the convention that
[W^{n}_{m}]=0
whenever
m<0
,
n<m
, or
m\not\equiv n\operatorname{mod}2
.

Let
\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}
be the subspace generated by
\{[W^{n}_{m}]|n\geq m\geq j\}
. This determines a filtration of
\mathcal{T\!L}
with
\mathcal{T\!L}_{j+1}\subset\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}
and
\mathcal{T\!L}_{-1}=\mathcal{T\!L}_{0}=\mathcal{T\!L}
. Now

(70)

\displaystyle[\operatorname{Ind}]\cdot\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}\subset\mathcal{T\!L}_{j-1},

\displaystyle[\operatorname{Res}]\cdot\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}\subset\mathcal{T\!L}_{j-1},

\displaystyle[P_{k}]\cdot\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}\subset\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}\,.

Remark 8.7
.

For
[W^{n}_{m}]\in\mathcal{T\!L}_{j}
,
[P_{k}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]=\delta_{m,n-2k}[W^{n}_{m}]
. If
[P_{k}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]
is nonzero, then
n\geq j+2k
.
∎

Definition 8.8
.

An
asymptotic representation
of a filtered algebra
i_{n}:A_{n}\hookrightarrow A_{n+1}
acting on a filtered vector space
j_{n+1}:V_{n+1}\hookrightarrow V_{n}
is a collection of linear maps
f_{n,m}:A_{n}\otimes V_{m}\to V_{m-n}
for
m\geq n\geq 0
satisfying the following axioms:

(71)

\displaystyle f_{n+1,m+1}\circ(i_{n}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{V_{m+1}})

\displaystyle=j_{m-n+1}\circ f_{n,m+1}:A_{n}\otimes V_{m+1}\to V_{m-n}\,,

(72)

\displaystyle f_{n,m}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{A_{n}}\otimes j_{m+1})

\displaystyle=j_{m-n+1}\circ f_{n,m+1}:A_{n}\otimes V_{m+1}\to V_{m-n}\,,

(73)

\displaystyle f_{n+l,m}\circ(\mu_{l,n}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{V_{m}})

\displaystyle=f_{l,m-n}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{A_{l}}\otimes f_{n,m}):A_{l}\otimes A_{n}\otimes V_{m}\to V_{m-n-l}\,,

where
m\geq n+l
and
\mu_{l,n}:A_{l}\otimes A_{n}\to A_{n+l}
is the multiplication map. These axioms are referred to as algebra coherence, vector space coherence, and composition respectively.

Proposition 8.9
.

The assignment
x\mapsto[\operatorname{Ind}]
,
y\mapsto[\operatorname{Res}]
,
c_{k}\mapsto[P_{k}]
defines an asymptotic representation of
\mathcal{K}
on
\mathcal{T\!L}
.

Proof.

Formally, the collection of maps
f_{n,m}:\mathcal{K}_{n}\otimes\mathcal{T\!L}_{m}\to\mathcal{T\!L}_{m-n}
are determined from the axioms by the assignments:

\displaystyle f_{0,m}:\mathcal{K}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{T\!L}_{m}\to\mathcal{T\!L}_{m}

\displaystyle{\begin{cases}c_{k}\otimes[W^{n}_{m}]\mapsto\delta_{m,n-2k}[W^{n}_{n-2k}]\end{cases}}

\displaystyle f_{1,m}:\mathcal{K}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{T\!L}_{m}\to\mathcal{T\!L}_{m-1}

\displaystyle\begin{cases}x\otimes[W^{n}_{m}]\mapsto[W^{n+1}_{m+1}]+[W^{n+1}_{m-1}]\\
y\otimes[W^{n}_{m}]\mapsto\overline{\delta_{n,m}}[W^{n-1}_{m+1}]+[W^{n-1}_{m-1}]\end{cases}

The axioms (
71
) and (
72
) of Definition
8.8
hold trivially. The composition axiom (
73
) determines
f_{n,m}
by expressing each element of
\mathcal{K}_{n}
as a word written in the generators of
\mathcal{K}
. It remains to check that two words in
\mathcal{K}_{n}
which are equivalent under the relations of
\mathcal{K}
have the same action under
f_{n,m}
.

The relations (
60
)-(
65
) are determined by classes of functors in the “generic” isomorphisms of Table
1
. As noted in Remark
5.7
, these isomorphisms hold in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{\mathbf{2Weyl}}}(n,-)
provided that
n>2k
, where
k
is an index of a functor
C_{k}
appearing in a given isomorphism. In particular, we are concerned with avoiding instances where a “generic” isomorphism fails, namely those which are labeled “none” in the table. The corresponding words in such relations belong to
\mathcal{K}_{2}
. By Remark
8.7
, if
W^{n}_{m}\in\mathcal{T\!L}_{2}
and
[P_{k}]\cdot[W^{n}_{m}]\neq 0
, then
n\geq 2k+2>2k
. Thus, the relations are indeed respected by the action. The remaining relations in
\mathcal{K}
are considered generic and are easily verified to hold under the asymptotic action.
∎

8.3.
Structure of
\mathcal{K}

Here we discuss additional relations and bases for certain subalgebras of
\mathcal{K}
. For later use, observe that there is an anti-automorphism
\phi:\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{K}
which exchanges
x
and
y
.

Lemma 8.10
.

Let
0\leq l_{1}\leq l_{2}\leq l_{3}
and
n,m\geq 0
. Then

\displaystyle c_{l_{3}}x^{n}c_{l_{2}}x^{m}c_{l_{1}}=\dfrac{{n\choose l_{3}-l_{2}}{m\choose l_{2}-l_{1}}}{{n+m\choose l_{3}-l_{1}}}c_{l_{3}}x^{n+m}c_{l_{1}}\,.

Proof.

Let
k_{0},k_{1},\dots,k_{n+m}
be any sequence such that
k_{i+1}\in\{k_{i},k_{i}+1\}
,
k_{0}=l_{1}
,
k_{m}=l_{2}
, and
k_{n+m}=l_{3}
. It follows from both (
60
) and (
62
), that

\displaystyle c_{l_{2}}x^{m}c_{l_{1}}={m\choose l_{2}-l_{1}}c_{k_{m}}\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}xc_{k_{i}}\,,\quad\quad c_{l_{3}}x^{n}c_{l_{2}}={n\choose l_{3}-l_{2}}c_{k_{n+m}}\prod_{i=m}^{m+n-1}xc_{k_{i}}\,,

\displaystyle c_{l_{3}}x^{n+m}c_{l_{1}}={n+m\choose l_{3}-l_{1}}c_{k_{n+m}}\prod_{i=0}^{m+n-1}xc_{k_{i}}\,.

Then

\displaystyle c_{l_{3}}x^{n}c_{l_{2}}x^{m}c_{l_{1}}

\displaystyle={n\choose l_{3}-l_{2}}{m\choose l_{2}-l_{1}}c_{k_{n+m}}\prod_{i=m}^{m+n-1}xc_{k_{i}}\cdot c_{k_{m}}\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}xc_{k_{i}}

\displaystyle={n\choose l_{3}-l_{2}}{m\choose l_{2}-l_{1}}c_{k_{n+m}}\prod_{i=0}^{m+n-1}xc_{k_{i}}=\dfrac{{n\choose l_{3}-l_{2}}{m\choose l_{2}-l_{1}}}{{n+m\choose l_{3}-l_{1}}}c_{l_{3}}x^{n+m}c_{l_{1}}\,.

∎

Remark 8.11
.

Lemma
8.10
readily implies an integral basis for the subalgebra generated by
\{c_{l_{2}}x^{m}c_{l_{1}}:l_{1},l_{2},m\geq 0\}
. This basis is spanned by “divided powers elements”
x^{(l_{2},m,l_{1})}\coloneq\dfrac{1}{{m\choose l_{1}-l_{2}}}c_{l_{2}}x^{m}c_{l_{1}}

with
l_{1}+m\geq l_{2}\geq l_{1}
, which multiply according to the rule
x^{(l_{4},n,l_{3})}x^{(l_{2},m,l_{1})}=\delta_{l_{3},l_{2}}x^{(l_{4},n+m,l_{1})}
.
∎

Introduce the notation

\displaystyle\{x\}^{n}_{l}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x^{i}c_{l-i}x^{n-i}

and

\displaystyle[x]^{n}_{l}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x^{i}c_{l-1}x^{n-i}\,.

It is then easy to verify that

(74)

\displaystyle\{x\}^{n+1}_{l}=x^{n+1}c_{l-{n+1}}+\{x\}^{n}_{l}\cdot x

and

\displaystyle[x]^{n+1}_{l}=x^{n+1}c_{l-1}+[x]^{n}_{l}\cdot x

Lemma 8.12
.

For nonnegative integers
l
and
n
, the following identity holds in
\mathcal{K}
:

yc_{l}x^{n}=c_{l}x^{n}yc_{l-n}+c_{l-1}x^{n}yc_{l}+c_{l}\{x\}^{n-1}_{l}+c_{l-1}[x]^{n-1}_{l}\,.

Proof.

We give a proof by induction on
n
. The claim is immediately verified in the case
n=0
. We then compute by the inductive hypothesis

\displaystyle yc_{l}x^{n+1}

\displaystyle=\left(c_{l}x^{n}yc_{l-n}+c_{l-1}x^{n}yc_{l}+c_{l}\{x\}^{n-1}_{l}+c_{l-1}[x]^{n-1}_{l}\right)x

\displaystyle=\left(c_{l}x^{n}c_{l-n}+c_{l}x^{n}c_{l-n}xyc_{l-n-1}\right)+\left(c_{l-1}x^{n}c_{l-1}+c_{l-1}x^{n}c_{l-1}xyc_{l}\right)+c_{l}\{x\}^{n-1}_{l}\cdot x+c_{l-1}[x]^{n-1}_{l}\cdot x

\displaystyle=c_{l}x^{n+1}yc_{l-n-1}+c_{l-1}x^{n+1}yc_{l}+c_{l}\{x\}^{n}_{l}+c_{l-1}[x]^{n}_{l}\,.

In the second equality we use that
c_{l}x^{n}c_{l-n-1}=c_{l-1}x^{n}c_{l}=0
. The third equality is due to the relations
c_{l}x^{n}c_{l-n}xyc_{l-n-1}=c_{l}x^{n+1}yc_{l-n-1}
,
c_{l-1}x^{n}c_{l-1}xyc_{l}=c_{l-1}x^{n+1}yc_{l}
, and those in (
74
). Thus, proving the claim.
∎

Lemma 8.13
.

For each
k\geq l\geq 0
,
c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{l}
is spanned by

S_{k,l}=\{c_{k}x^{k-l+m}c_{l},c_{k}x^{k-l}y^{m}c_{l}\mid m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\}\,.

Proof.

Fix
k\geq 0
. For each word
w\in\mathcal{K}
let
\ell(w)
be the length of
w
(not necessarily a reduced word). We give an inductive proof on the length of
w
and a downward induction on
l
. For a given word
w
, observe that if
k-l>\ell(w)
, then
c_{k+l}wc_{k}=0
and if
k-l=\ell(w)
, then
c_{k+l}wc_{k}
is nonzero exactly when
w=x^{k-l}
. The base case for a word of length
1
is immediate.

Assume for any word
w
of length at most
n
and any
k-n\geq l\geq 0
that
c_{k}wc_{l}\in\operatorname{span}(S_{k,l})
. Fix a word
w
of length
n+1
. The base case of the downward induction is
l=k-(n+1)
as described above. Now fix that
c_{k}wc_{l}\in\operatorname{span}(S_{k,l})
. We now show that
c_{k}wc_{l-1}\in\operatorname{span}(S_{k,l-1})
. We proceed in cases, assuming that
w=w_{1}w^{\prime}
where
w_{1}\in\{c_{l-1},x,y\}
and
\ell(w^{\prime})=n
.

The case
w_{1}=c_{l-1}
is the simplest as
c_{k}wc_{l-1}=c_{k}w^{\prime}c_{l-1}
and belongs to
\operatorname{span}(S_{k,l-1})
by the inductive hypothesis. Note that if
w_{1}
is equal to any other
c_{s}
, then
c_{k}wc_{l-1}=0
.

Next, suppose
w_{1}=x
. Then

\displaystyle c_{k}wc_{l-1}=

\displaystyle~c_{k}xw^{\prime}c_{l-1}=c_{k}xc_{k}w^{\prime}c_{l-1}+c_{k}xc_{k-1}w^{\prime}c_{l-1}

\displaystyle\sum_{m}a_{m}c_{k}xc_{k}x^{k-l+1+m}c_{l-1}+\sum_{m}a^{\prime}_{m}c_{k}xc_{k-1}x^{k-l}y^{m}c_{l-1}

\displaystyle+\sum_{m}b_{m}c_{k}xc_{k-1}x^{k-l+m}c_{l-1}+\sum_{m}b^{\prime}_{m}c_{k}xc_{k}x^{k-l+1}y^{m}c_{l-1}

for some coefficients,
a_{m},a^{\prime}_{m},b_{m},b^{\prime}_{m}\in{\mathbb{C}}(q)
. The resulting (finite) sums may be expressed in the desired basis by first writing
c_{k^{\prime}}x^{k^{\prime}-l+1}y^{m}c_{l-1}=c_{k^{\prime}}x^{k^{\prime}-l+1}c_{k^{\prime}}y^{m}c_{l-1}
for the sums involving
y^{m}
terms, then applying Lemma
8.10
to all four sums.

Finally, consider
w_{1}=y
. We have

\displaystyle c_{k}wc_{l-1}

\displaystyle~=c_{k}yw^{\prime}c_{l-1}=c_{k}yc_{k}w^{\prime}c_{l-1}+c_{k}yc_{k+1}w^{\prime}c_{l-1}

\displaystyle\sum_{m}a_{m}c_{k}yc_{k}x^{k-l+1+m}c_{l-1}+\sum_{m}a^{\prime}_{m}c_{k}yc_{k}x^{k-l+1}y^{m}c_{l-1}

\displaystyle+\sum_{m}b_{m}c_{k}yc_{k+1}x^{k-l+2+m}c_{l-1}+\sum_{m}b^{\prime}_{m}c_{k}yc_{k+1}x^{k-l+2}y^{m}c_{l-1}

for some coefficients,
a_{m},a^{\prime}_{m},b_{m},b^{\prime}_{m}\in{\mathbb{C}}(q)
. The claim follows from Lemmas
8.12
and
8.10
.
∎

Lemma 8.14
.

For each
k\geq l\geq 0
,
S_{k,l}
is a basis for
c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{l}
.

Proof.

Let
\delta=k-l\geq 0
. We prove that
S_{k,l}
is a linearly independent set. Assume for a contradiction that there is a linear dependence

\displaystyle d=\sum_{m}a_{m}c_{k}x^{\delta+m}c_{l}+b_{m}c_{k}x^{\delta}y^{m}c_{l}=0\,.

for some coefficients
a_{m},b_{m}\in{\mathbb{C}}(q)
. Let
M
be the largest
m
such that
a_{m}
and
b_{m}
are nonzero. Thus,
d\in\mathcal{K}_{M+\delta}
and we may consider its action on
\mathcal{T\!L}_{M+\delta}
since
\mathcal{K}
acts asymptotically on
\mathcal{T\!L}
. Consider
[W^{M+k+l}_{M+\delta}]\in\mathcal{T\!L}_{M+\delta}
so that

\displaystyle c_{k}x^{\delta+m}c_{l}\cdot[W^{M+k+l}_{M+\delta}]

\displaystyle=c_{k}x^{\delta+m}\cdot[W^{M+k+l}_{M+k-l}]={l+m\choose l}[W^{M+2k+m}_{M+m}]

\displaystyle c_{k}x^{\delta}y^{m}c_{l}\cdot[W^{M+k+l}_{M+\delta}]

\displaystyle=c_{k}x^{\delta}c_{l}y^{m}c_{l}\cdot[W^{M+k+l}_{M+k-l}]=c_{k}x^{\delta}\cdot[W^{M-m+k+l}_{M-m+k-l}]=[W^{M+2k-m}_{M-m}]

Since each term in
d
maps
[W^{M+k+l}_{M+\delta}]
to a unique nonzero vector in
\mathcal{T\!L}
, the linear dependence must be the trivial one.
∎

Remark 8.15
.

By applying the anti-automorphism
\phi
which switches
x
and
y
, there is a basis of
c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{l}
for
k\geq l\geq 0
given by
S_{l,k}=\{c_{l}y^{(k-l)+m}c_{k},c_{l}y^{k-l}x^{m}c_{k}\mid m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}\}
.
∎

For integers
k,l,m\geq 0
, define

\displaystyle X^{m}_{k,l}\coloneq\begin{cases}c_{k}x^{m+(k-l)}c_{l}/{m+(k-l)\choose k-l}&k\geq l\\
c_{k}x^{m}y^{l-k}c_{l}&l\geq k\end{cases}\,,

\displaystyle X^{-m}_{l,k}\coloneq\phi(X^{m}_{k,l})\,.

The choice of asymmetric normalization is intentional.

Lemma 8.16
.

For
a,b\geq 0
and
n,m\in{\mathbb{Z}}
, the multiplication map
c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{l}\otimes c_{l}\mathcal{K}c_{k}\to c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{k}
satisfies

X^{n}_{k,l}\otimes X^{m}_{l,k}\mapsto X^{n+m}_{k,k}.

Proof.

The proof is a direct computation for choices
k\geq l
or
l\geq k
,
n\geq 0
or
n\leq 0
, and
m\geq 0
or
m\leq 0
. We include one such computation. Assume
k\leq l
and
m,n\geq 0
. Then

\displaystyle X^{n}_{k,l}X^{m}_{l,k}=c_{k}x^{n}y^{l-k}c_{l}x^{m+l-k}c_{l}/{m+l-k\choose l-k}=c_{k}x^{n}c_{k}y^{l-k}c_{l}x^{l-k}c_{k}x^{m}c_{k}=c_{k}x^{n}c_{k}x^{m}c_{k}=X^{n+m}_{k,k}\,.

∎

Corollary 8.17
.

For each
k\geq 0
,
c_{k}\mathcal{K}c_{k}
is isomorphic to a Laurent polynomial algebra in the variable
X_{k,k}
.

Appendix A
Results from Quinn

We recall key statements and main results from
[
Qui17
]
which we use in this paper. Namely, the structure of the representation categories of Temperley-Lieb algebras, the action of induction and restriction functors, and relations in the precursor to the universal Weyl category. The reader is referred there and references therein for additional details. Unless stated otherwise, results given here are proven in
[
Qui17
]
. Some notation is changed in this paper.

A.1.
Representations of Temperley-Lieb Algebras

The set of isomorphism classes of irreducible
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
representations are in bijection with nonnegative integers
m\leq n
such that
m\equiv n\operatorname{mod}2
. We denote such an irreducible representation
W^{n}_{m}
. Vectors in these representations may be presented as
(m,n)
-Temperley-Lieb diagrams
w
such that
w=wf^{(m)}
. This implies that
W^{n}_{n}
is the trivial representation. We assume that
W^{n}_{m}=0
is
m
is negative, exceeds
n
, or has different parity from
n
.

A basis for these representations is given using a path algebra approach. Equivalently, there is a Young tableaux description of basis vectors given in
[
Moo18
]
, for example. Let
P^{n}
denote the set of paths of length
n
starting from the vertex labeled
1
on the type
\mathsf{A}_{n+1}
graph whose vertices are labeled
0,1,2,\dots,n
. A path of length
n
is notated by a sequence
p=(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n})
of nonnegative integers such that
p_{1}=1
and
p_{i+1}=p_{i}\pm 1
for
i<n
. A basis for
W^{n}_{m}
is in bijection with
P^{n}_{m}
the set of paths in
P^{n}
which end at vertex
m
, i.e,
p_{n}=m
. For a given path, the corresponding basis element is constructed inductively from a single strand. Suppose that
v_{k}
is the
(p_{k},k)
-Temperley-Lieb diagram constructed from a path of length
k
ending at
p_{k}
. If the path continues to the right (increases), then

The normalization factor
\sqrt{\frac{[p_{k}]}{[p_{k}+1]}}
is required for orthonormality in the following sense. If
p\in P^{n}_{m}
corresponds to
v_{p}\in W^{n}_{m}
, then the reflection of
v_{p}
over a horizontal axis is the corresponding dual basis vector
\check{v}_{p}
in the sense that
\check{v}_{p}(v_{r})=\delta_{p,r}
, where
\delta=1
if
p=r
and is zero otherwise. Write
e_{p,r}
for the matrix element
v_{p}\check{v}_{r}
provided
p,r\in P^{n}_{m}
.

Remark A.1
.

We observe that
\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{m}}e_{p,p}\in\operatorname{TL}_{n}
is an idempotent corresponding to the projection onto
W^{n}_{m}
. Moreover,

\displaystyle\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{m}}e_{p,p}=\sum_{r\in P^{n-1}_{m+1}}\frac{[m+1]}{[m+2]}v_{r}e_{n-1}^{\prime}\check{v}_{r}+\sum_{r\in P^{n-1}_{m-1}}v_{r}f^{(m)}\check{v}_{r}.

A.2.
Induction and Restriction for Temperley-Lieb Modules

For any
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-module
V
, the induction functor may be defined as the functor

(77)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Ind}:\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}\to\operatorname{TL}_{n+1}\mathrm{-mod}

\displaystyle V\mapsto{}_{n+1}(n+1)_{n}\otimes V

or informally as adding an additional string to the diagram. Restriction is instead given by the functor

(78)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Res}:\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}\to\operatorname{TL}_{n-1}\mathrm{-mod}

\displaystyle V\mapsto{}_{n-1}(n)_{n}\otimes V

which in some sense forgets the
n
-th string in the diagram.

Quinn provides a formula for the restriction of (nonzero) simple modules
W^{n}_{m}
in terms of simple modules
\operatorname{Res}(W^{n}_{m})\cong W^{n-1}_{m+1}\oplus W^{n-1}_{m-1}
. The isomorphism is
witnessed by the maps:

(79)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Res}(W^{n}_{m})\to W^{n-1}_{m+1}\oplus W^{n-1}_{m-1}:

Remark A.2
.

The vectors appearing in the image of (
81
), together with their dual vectors, agree with the decomposition of
\sum_{p\in P^{n}_{m}}e_{p,p}
given in Remark
A.1
. Our previous observation is therefore an expression of the projection onto
W^{n}_{m}
in terms of projections through components of
\operatorname{Ind}(W^{n-1}_{m+1})
and
\operatorname{Ind}(W^{n-1}_{m-1})
.
∎

A.3.
Diagrammatic Calculus

In Chapter 5, Quinn initiates the definition of the Weyl category. An important difference in our notation is that Quinn’s crossing is replaced by
[2]
times the cupcap. It acts by multiplication by
e^{\prime}
, the pre-idempotent Temperley-Lieb generator, on the two induced strands. Quinn defines an abstract category which acts on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}
-modules in the following way

(83)

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\otimes y\mapsto xy\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n-1}(n)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n)_{n},

(84)

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto x\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n+1)_{n+1}(n+1)_{n},

(85)

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x)\right]:{}_{n}(n+1)_{n+1}(n+1)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n)_{n},

(86)

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,r\in P^{n}\\
p_{n}=r_{n}\end{subarray}}c_{r}e_{p,r}\otimes e_{r,p}x\right]:{}_{n}(n)_{n}\to{}_{n}(n)_{n-1}(n)_{n},

(87)

\displaystyle\overset{n}{=}\left[x\mapsto xe_{n+1}\right]:{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n}\to{}_{n+2}(n+2)_{n}

where the map
x\mapsto\operatorname{ptr}_{n+1}(x)
is the right partial trace of
x
as defined in (
4
),
e_{p,r}
and
e_{r,p}
are the matrix units defined here in Section
A.1
, and

c_{r}=\frac{[r_{n-1}+1]}{[r_{n}+1]}\frac{1}{|P^{n}_{r_{n-1}}|}
.

Quinn showed that these generators satisfy the following relations for any
n\geq 0
in the action on
\operatorname{TL}_{n}\mathrm{-mod}
. The proof of (
88
) is given in
[
Qui17
, Theorem 4.2.14]
.
